concept: Why does a population grow fast and then level off?
title: Crowded Pond
tagline: Start small, grow fast, then why does the pond push back?

science.hiddenLaw: Logistic growth with carrying capacity: dN/dt = rN(1 - N/K); the per-capita growth rate declines linearly with density (r*(1-N/K)) due to density-dependent resource limitation, producing exponential growth when N << K and zero net growth (births ≈ deaths) as N → K.
science.plainStatement: When a population is small, resources are abundant and it grows fast; as it gets crowded, each individual gets fewer resources so growth slows, until births balance deaths and the population levels off at the carrying capacity the environment can support.
misconceptions: Populations will keep growing exponentially forever as long as birth rate exceeds death rate — ignoring that resources are finite.
Leveling off means reproduction stops completely (birth rate goes to zero), rather than births continuing but becoming equal to deaths so net growth is zero.
Carrying capacity (K) is set by the starting population size or is the same everywhere, rather than by environmental resources and density-dependent competition.
Growth slows only because individuals get old and die more, not because crowding reduces per-capita resources and lowers birth rates / raises death rates in a density-dependent way.

checks.description: At low density (N << K) per-capita growth rate ≈ r, showing initial exponential phase
Population starting well below K levels off near K=500 and net growth approaches zero
Higher carrying capacity produces higher final population - plateau at K=1000 vs 500
Control: remove density dependence → leveling off disappears and population keeps growing exponentially
At carrying capacity net growth is zero but births continue (births ≈ deaths >0), refuting 'reproduction stops' misconception
